question: Clap along to almost any pop song and your hands land on beats 2 and 4. Why not on 1 and 3?
answer: Because the kick already owns 1 and 3. A snare on the weak beats answers each low thump with a high crack, so every bar pushes away from where its weight lies. Earl Palmer, the drummer on Little Richard's hits, said he learned to clap on 2 and 4 behind New Orleans parade bands.
move: Put the accent where nothing else is already pushing.
ask: Where would my effort count more if I put it where nobody else is?

scene.hint: Kick and hat are playing. Add a snare on 1 and 3, then swap it for 2 and 4.

tracks.name: Hat
tracks.pattern: x . x . x . x . x . x . x . x .

tracks.text: Snare on top of the kick: every hit lands on the strong beat. A march.
Low thump, high crack, low thump, high crack: the backbeat. Now it rocks.

moments.name: Every beat
moments.text: Snare on all four: the crack loses its contrast, and the push goes flat.

reference: Tony Scherman, Backbeat: Earl Palmer's Story, Smithsonian Institution Press, 1999; 64 Parishes, Earl Palmer (clapping on 2 and 4 behind Treme brass bands)
